name: Malacca
info: Malacca City is the capital of the Malaysian state of Malacca, on the Strait of Malacca. Parameswara founded it, according to tradition in 1396, and it became a great entrepôt before Portuguese, Dutch and British rule.

facts.founded: Founded by Parameswara, a Sumatran prince; 1396 is the year in which he announced the name Malaka, after a legend of a mouse deer and a tree.
facts.where: On both sides of the Malacca River near its mouth on the Strait of Malacca, on the south-western coast of the Malay Peninsula, in Malaysia, about 152 km from Kuala Lumpur.
facts.known: The Malacca Sultanate and its entrepôt; ties with Ming China and Zheng He; conquest by the Portuguese in 1511; the fortress A Famosa; the Dutch capture of 1641; the Straits Settlements; the Peranakan, Chitty and Kristang communities
facts.today: Malacca City is the capital of the Malaysian state of Malacca, and its historic core, with George Town, was listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2008.

t: Parameswara, a Sumatran prince who had left Palembang and then Temasek, founded the city at a fishing village at the mouth of the Malacca River, and Ming China's protection kept Siam and Majapahit from conquering it.

The Portuguese took it in 1511 and built the fortress A Famosa, the Dutch took it from them in 1641 with the help of Johor, and in 1824 the British and Dutch agreed that it would pass to Britain, which handed over in 1825.
Under the British it was part of the Straits Settlements, the Japanese occupied it from 1942 to 1945, and Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957.
dyk: According to legend, Parameswara named the city after the tree under which he was resting when he saw a tiny mouse deer kick his follower's hunting dogs into a river.
ev: Parameswara announces that the place will be called Malaka
The first official Chinese trade envoy, Admiral Yin Qing, arrives
Zheng He brings a stone tablet and an imperial order raising the port to a country
The Portuguese under Afonso de Albuquerque capture the city
The Dutch East India Company, with Johor, take Malacca from the Portuguese
An Anglo-Dutch treaty places Malacca in British hands, and it is handed over in 1825
Japanese forces enter the city and occupy it until 1945

sections.origins:
Malacca City stands on both sides of the Malacca River near its mouth on the Strait of Malacca, on flat and gently undulating land. Parameswara, a Sumatran prince, escaped from Palembang after Srivijaya fell to the Javanese Majapahit in 1377 and decided to build a new kingdom. He first settled at Temasek, where he killed Temagi, a regent who served under the Siamese king. Fearing reprisals from Siam, he left, and Temasek was then attacked by Majapahit. At Muar he tried two sites, Biawak Busuk and Kota Buruk, and found them unsuitable. He reportedly visited Sening Ujong before he reached a Malay fishing village at the mouth of the Bertam River, now the Malacca River.

According to the legend he rested there under a tree called the Malacca tree, and saw a tiny mouse deer kick his follower's hunting dogs into the river. Amused, he decided that the place must be unusual, and in 1396 he announced that it would be called Malaka. Two other accounts of the name exist. Tomé Pires, in the Suma Oriental, explained it as a term for a fugitive, reflecting Parameswara's own history, and the Malay Annals suggest that Arab merchants called the kingdom Malakat, meaning a congregation of merchants, in the reign of Muhammad Shah (1424 to 1444). Under the Portuguese the name was spelled Malaca, under the Dutch Malakka or Malacka, and under the British Malacca.
sections.growth:
The site soon became the centre of the Malay world in the 15th and 16th centuries and the most prosperous entrepôt in the Malay Archipelago. In 1403 the first official Chinese trade envoy, Admiral Yin Qing, arrived, and Parameswara was later escorted on his visits by Zheng He and other envoys. According to Ma Huan and Fei Xin, Malacca had been a relatively insignificant place before these voyages, not even a polity, and a vassal of Siam. In 1405 the Ming court sent Zheng He with a stone tablet enfeoffing the Western Mountain of Malacca and an imperial order raising the port to the status of a country. The Chinese built a government depot as a fortified cantonment for their soldiers, and Ma Huan reported that Siam did not dare to invade afterwards.

Ma Huan described a city surrounded by a palisade with four gates and watch towers, and inside it a second fortification holding the merchants' godowns, the treasury and the food storehouses. The river divided the city into two almost equal halves, the south being the inner citadel and the ruler's compound and the north, reached by a bridge, holding the many foreign merchants. About a score of market stalls stood on the bridge, near the docks where foreign ships unloaded.

Traders specialised by origin: the Gujaratis, Tamils and Bengalis were mostly cloth merchants, the Chinese dealt in silk, camphor and porcelain, the Bugis and other islanders in spices and sandalwood, the Minangkabau in pepper and gold, and the Javanese controlled rice and imported foodstuffs.
sections.rulers:
Parameswara founded the city and the Malacca Sultanate. Because of the influence of Arab, Persian and Indian traders it became an Islamic sultanate, and Parameswara converted when he married a princess from Pasai, taking the name Sultan Iskandar Shah. He paid tribute in person to the Chinese emperor in 1411 and died in 1414. His son Megat Iskandar Shah succeeded him. Muhammad Shah reigned from 1424 to 1444, Mansur Shah from 1456 to 1477, and Mahmud Shah was the eighth sultan.

In 1511 the Portuguese took the city. They held it until 1641, when the Dutch East India Company (VOC), which had made a treaty with Johor, captured it. The Dutch enlarged the fort and built a good deal of new infrastructure, and Malacca was placed under the direct control of Batavia in Java. From 1796 to 1801 and from 1807 to 1818 it was placed under a British Resident while the Netherlands was under French conquest, and it was returned to the Dutch in 1818.

A treaty of 1824 between Britain and the Netherlands led to the city's being handed to the British in 1825, and it became part of the Straits Settlements under a Resident at Penang. The Japanese occupied it from 1942 to 1945. It was then administered by the British Military Administration, and then under the Malayan Union and the Federation of Malaya. Malaya became independent on 31 August 1957, and the Federation of Malaysia was formed in 1963.
sections.life:
The city's people have long been of many origins. In the sultanate period a Hindu-Malay and a Tamil-Malay society formed. The Chinese occupied the south-east side of the port around Bukit Cina, where they built temples and a well called Hang Li Poh's Well. According to local folklore Hang Li Po, a daughter of the Ming emperor, arrived with 500 attendants to marry Sultan Mansur Shah, and the attendants married locals and settled mostly at Bukit Cina. She is also named as the fifth wife of the sixth sultan.

Because of marriage between communities since the sultanate, the city has its own mixed peoples. The Baba Nyonya are Straits-born Chinese who have lived there for generations as traders and married local Malay women, adopting the Malay language and local culture while keeping some Chinese traditions. The Chitty descend from Indian traders and local women of Malay, Javanese, Batak and Chinese origin. The Kristang descend from Portuguese men and Malay, Chinese and Indian women of the Portuguese period. Malay, Hokkien and English are the main languages, and the Baba Nyonya, Chitty and Kristang each have a creole of their own.

In the census of 2010 the city had 484,885 people: 273,844 Malays, 158,828 Chinese, 20,310 Indians, 9,732 others and about 22,171 non-citizens. Most Malays were Muslims, the Chinese mostly Buddhists, Confucianists, Taoists or followers of Chinese folk religion, the Indians mainly Hindus and the Kristang mostly Christians. The Portuguese built churches, convents and a bishop's palace, and the Dutch Square holds the Stadthuys and Christ Church.
sections.crises:
The Portuguese came for the trade. Their envoy Diogo Lopes de Sequeira was first well received by Sultan Mahmud Shah, but the Tamil Muslim community, citing the Portuguese treatment of the Muslims of Goa, persuaded the sultan to act against them, and he had several of the delegation captured and killed. In April 1511 Afonso de Albuquerque arrived with an armada. He wished to cut off Islamic and Venetian trade, and he said that if Malacca were taken out of the hands of the Moors, Cairo and Mecca would be ruined. A first attack on 25 July 1511 failed, and a second succeeded in August 1511.

The Portuguese built the fortress A Famosa from stone taken from Muslim graves, mosques and other buildings. They imposed higher taxes on Chinese traders and restricted their ownership of land. Aceh and Johor then fought each other and the Portuguese for the city, in attacks in 1564, 1570, 1613 and 1623 and a triangular war, until a large armada from Goa came to defend Malacca and destroyed the sultanate. The Dutch and Johor then took the city from the Portuguese in 1641.

When Japan took Malaya, news of the sinking of the Prince of Wales and Repulse on 10 December 1941 caused panic, British officials fled, and thousands of residents hid in rubber estates and jungle. The Japanese army arrived on 14 January 1942 and there was no major battle. The Kempeitai used the former Government Rest House for arrests, torture and executions, rice rations were low, and a number of residents were taken to build the Burma-Siam Railway. The city was left undamaged when Japan surrendered in August 1945.
sections.legacy:
The Portuguese, Dutch and British each left marks on the city. The Dutch Square is surrounded by Dutch buildings such as the Stadthuys and Christ Church, and the Portuguese traces are mostly the Porta de Santiago and St Peter's Church. The British dismantled the old fort and made rules for infrastructure that produced back alleys, back yards, fire escapes and pedestrian arcades. The historic central area lies near the old coastline, with St Paul's Hill and the ruins of the Portuguese fortress and the Dutch Square on the eastern bank of the river and the old Chinatown on the western.

The communities that grew from the city's history keep their traditions: the Peranakan Chinese in Chinatown, the Chitty and the Kristang, whose Portuguese Settlement is the centre of Portuguese culture, with many Eurasians descended from Portuguese men and local women. The Kuomintang Cenotaph on Bukit Cina commemorates thousands of Chinese in Malacca who were killed by the Japanese during the occupation. The Padang Pahlawan is the site where Tunku Abdul Rahman made his first announcement of independence.

Malacca was given the title of Historical City on 15 April 1989, was granted city status on 15 April 2003, and on 7 July 2008 was listed, with George Town in the north of the peninsula, as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its council area was set at 270 square kilometres after land reclamation carried out since 1974, and the city today is the political and economic centre of the state of Malacca.

summary: Malacca City, on the Strait of Malacca, was founded by the Sumatran prince Parameswara in 1396, and became a great entrepôt protected by Ming China. The Portuguese took it in 1511, the Dutch in 1641 and the British in 1825. It is the capital of the Malaysian state of Malacca.
notes: SOURCES: the city article (wp2/malacca-city.txt) and the state article (wp/malacca.txt). Everything about the state's districts, government, area, population and the Naning War, Dondang Sayang, Malacca High School, the governor and the 2020 state census was dropped. Facts used only from the state article: the Dutch capture on 14 January 1641 after a long siege (the city article gives no date), the Francis Xavier visits (dropped), the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 in exchange for Bencoolen (dropped, the city article says only that the 1824 treaty led to a handover in 1825), and the Malayan Union and Federation of Malaya dates.

CONFLICT, founding: the city article says Parameswara announced the name Malaka in 1396 and that the city was founded in 1396; the state article gives no founding date and its draft used 1403 (first Chinese envoy). I used 1396 with circa true as the city article's own year. The city article also says Srivijaya fell in 1377 and that Parameswara fled Palembang via Temasek and Muar; the state article says he fled a Majapahit invasion of Singapura. I followed the city article.

CONFLICT, 1511: the city article says the Portuguese took the city on 15 August 1511 after a failed attack on 25 July; the state article says 24 August 1511. I wrote 'August 1511' with no day, and the first attack of 25 July only from the city article.

CONFLICT, Hang Li Po: the state article says she is associated in local chronicles with the Ming court; the city article says folklore calls her a daughter of the Ming emperor and also, further down, the fifth wife of the sixth sultan Mansur Shah. I attributed it to local folklore. Note also that the city article names the ruler as 'Manshur Shah' in one place and 'Mansur Shah' in another, and calls him the sixth sultan.
Parameswara's conversion and his death in 1414 are in the city article only. The article says in one sentence that Mahmud Shah was 'the eighth Sultanate of Malacca'; I wrote 'eighth sultan'.
The city article says 'the city was founded in 1396 by Parameswara' while the Malacca Sultanate was established in 1400; I used only the founding year.

Left out as tourism, sports, transport, health care, courts, climate, twin towns, shopping and the present economy. The city's present population figure ('As of 2019 579,000') was left out as an 'as of' figure; the 2010 census figures are given with their year.

Intro of the city article says the Dutch took the city 'with Johor'; the details of Johor's treaty are as given. The article's statement that Malacca 'was a vassal region of Siam' comes from Ma Huan and Fei Xin as the article presents them.

The 1511 conquest: 1,200 men and 17 or 18 ships appear in the state article only and were left out. The Dutch capture year 1641 is in the city article only as an implied fact (the Portuguese, state article), so the date 14 January 1641 was left out of the text; the year appears in the facts, takeaways and events.

Treaty of 1824: the city article says the treaty was signed 'to prevent further British influence in Java' and that Malacca was 'officially handed to the British in 1825'; the event is labelled 1824 and says handover in 1825.
